body:
1. Muscular Tissue Produces Movement

Muscular tissue consists of specialised cells capable of contraction and relaxation. These cells contain contractile proteins that enable them to shorten or develop force.

Muscular tissue produces movements such as walking, changes in the diameter of internal tubes, movement of food through the digestive tract and pumping of blood by the heart.

At the school level, muscular tissue is classified into skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.

2. Skeletal or Striated Muscle

Skeletal muscle is generally attached to bones and contributes to voluntary movements such as lifting an arm or walking.

Its muscle fibres are long, cylindrical and unbranched. Each mature skeletal muscle fibre generally contains many nuclei.

Under the microscope, skeletal muscle shows alternating light and dark bands called striations. For this reason it is also called striated muscle.

Most skeletal movements are under voluntary control, although skeletal muscles may also participate in automatic responses.

3. Smooth or Unstriated Muscle

Smooth muscle occurs in the walls of several internal organs, including the alimentary canal, blood vessels and urinary passages.

Its cells are usually spindle-shaped, with tapering ends and a single nucleus. They do not show the conspicuous striations characteristic of skeletal muscle.

Smooth muscle generally acts without conscious control and is therefore described as involuntary muscle.

For example, waves of smooth-muscle contraction help move food along the digestive tract.

4. Cardiac Muscle

Cardiac muscle forms the muscular wall of the heart. Its repeated rhythmic contractions help pump blood through the circulatory system.

Cardiac muscle cells are branched, generally have 1 central nucleus and show striations. Their activity is involuntary.

Cardiac muscle therefore combines characteristics that should not be confused: it is striated but involuntary.

5. Comparison of the 3 Muscle Types

FeatureSkeletal muscleSmooth muscleCardiac muscle
Cell shapeLong, cylindricalSpindle-shapedBranched
StriationsPresentAbsentPresent
NucleiMany per fibreUsually 1Usually 1
ControlGenerally voluntaryInvoluntaryInvoluntary
Typical locationAttached to bonesInternal organ wallsHeart wall

Striated does not always mean voluntary. Both skeletal and cardiac muscles are striated, but cardiac muscle is involuntary.

6. Nervous Tissue

Nervous tissue is specialised for receiving information and transmitting signals. It is important for sensation, coordination and the control of responses.

The brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerves contain nervous tissue. Its principal signalling cells are called neurons, or nerve cells.

7. Structure of a Neuron

A typical neuron contains a cell body and specialised extensions.

  • Cell body: Contains the nucleus and much of the cytoplasm and supports cellular activities.
  • Dendrites: Usually short, branched processes specialised for receiving signals from other cells.
  • Axon: Usually a single long process that carries nerve impulses away from the cell body towards other cells.
  • Axon terminals: The ending branches through which a neuron communicates with another neuron, muscle cell or gland cell.

A nerve impulse is an electrical signal transmitted along a nerve cell. Nervous tissue enables the body to receive information and coordinate suitable responses.

8. Neuron and Nerve Are Different Terms

A neuron is an individual specialised nerve cell. A nerve is a structure containing bundles of nerve fibres, together with supporting connective tissues.

Therefore, a nerve should not be described as merely a single neuron.

9. Coordination Between Nervous and Muscular Tissues

Nervous and muscular tissues cooperate to produce many responses. For example, when a person voluntarily reaches for an object, nervous signals activate appropriate skeletal muscles, causing coordinated movement.

When food moves through the alimentary canal, smooth-muscle contractions are coordinated by nervous and other control mechanisms.

The important distinction is that nervous tissue transmits signals, while muscular tissue produces force through contraction.

10. Bringing Cell Biology and Tissues Together

Cells contain structures such as membranes, nuclei, ribosomes and mitochondria that support cellular functions. In multicellular organisms, cells become specialised and cooperate in tissues.

Plant tissues include actively dividing meristems and permanent tissues involved in support, storage, protection and transport. Animal tissues include epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues.

The distinction between plant and animal tissue organisation reflects their different functional requirements. Plants require localised growth and strong structural support, while animals often require coordinated movement and rapid responses to their surroundings.

The broader biological organisation is cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism. Each level depends on the structures and functions of the preceding level.

Prelims focus

  • Skeletal muscle is generally voluntary, striated and multinucleate.
  • Smooth muscle is involuntary, unstriated and usually uninucleate.
  • Cardiac muscle is involuntary, branched and striated.
  • Dendrites mainly receive signals; axons conduct impulses away from the cell body.
  • Nervous tissue transmits signals, while muscular tissue produces contraction.
  • Trap: Cardiac muscle has striations but is not under normal voluntary control.
